## Overview

The Stó꞉lō are First Nations peoples who inhabit the Fraser Valley and lower Fraser Canyon of British Columbia, Canada, within the loose grouping of Coast Salish nations. *Stó꞉lō* is the Halqemeylem word for “river,” and the Stó꞉lō are therefore described as the river people. Their traditional territory is called *S'ólh Téméxw*. The first traces of people living in the Fraser Valley date from 4,000 to 10,000 years ago. Stó꞉lō communities historically depended on fishing, foraging, hunting, and the harvesting of land and river resources. Their culture includes Halq'eméylem language traditions, longhouse life, salmon ceremonies, oral accounts of ancestral transformations, puberty rites, and systems of family status and leadership.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

The account of St. Mary's Indian Residential School states that students were given two sets of clothes, which were marked. The sources also describe students being assigned lockers, beds, and dormitory spaces and being checked for lice on arrival, but these details concern institutional life rather than Stó꞉lō dress traditions.

### Architecture

The primary shelter of the Stó꞉lō was the longhouse. Entire extended families lived in a longhouse, and the structure could be extended as the family expanded. Most Stó꞉lō longhouses had a single flat but slanted roof, although some modern longhouses were built with gabled roofs. The Xá꞉ytem Longhouse is given as an example of the traditional form. Pit houses, also called Quiggly hole houses, were used during earlier generations. Archaeological evidence from Xá:ytem records posthole and timber-frame construction, while the Fraser Valley Pyramids or Scowlitz Mounds at Harrison Bay contained timber structures supporting the weight of the mound.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Archaeological evidence records decorative and sculpted stone items, slate knives, slate points, hand mauls, nephrite chisels, and nephrite adzes. The early period also includes evidence of tools and timber-frame construction. River and lake canoes were built within Stó꞉lō communities, while larger ocean-going canoes were primarily acquired through trade with Indigenous peoples of the coast and Vancouver Island.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They mention decorative and sculpted stone items archaeologically.

## Music & performance

Singing and prayer formed part of traditional responses to illness during the smallpox epidemic. The sources state that people gathered around the sick person’s bed to sing and pray, a practice that exposed additional people to the virus. No named Stó꞉lō musical instruments, song genres, dance songs, secular performance forms, or professional performers are identified.

The sources describe oral tradition as central to Stó꞉lō culture. Accounts of arrival in *S'ólh Téméxw* describe people as *Tel Swayel*, or “sky-born” people, and *Tel Temexw*, or “earth-born” people. They also describe transformations of ancestral animals and fish, including the beaver, mountain goat, and sturgeon. *Xexá:ls*, described as transformers, fixed the world, the people, and the animals in it, creating the present landscape. These accounts connect performance, memory, place, and spiritual knowledge.

## Festivals & rituals

The First Salmon Ceremony was held when the first salmon were brought back from the river. The fish was shared with the entire community or more privately within a family setting. After the salmon meat was eaten, its bones were returned to the river to show respect to the salmon people. The sources state that if the ceremony was not performed and the fish was not shared, the fisher would experience bad luck for the rest of the year and the salmon run might not be as strong. They describe salmon as central to community life and state that ceremonies reflected its importance in Stó꞉lō culture.

A documented coming-of-age practice concerned girls at the time of their first menstruation. A pubescent girl was brought to a pit lined with cedar boughs and remained there during daylight hours, leaving only to eat and sleep. Women brought her fir boughs and instructed her to pick out the needles one at a time. This was the only work she was allowed to do; other women fed and washed her until her first menstrual period was over. The custom was practiced widely at least until youth were sent to residential schools.

## Foodways

Salmon was the preferred food of the Stó꞉lō and was regarded as superior to other kinds of meat. Salmon was said to give individuals energy, while meat made people feel heavy and lazy. Stó꞉lō communities fished on the Fraser River and its tributaries, including the Chilliwack and Harrison rivers. The First Salmon Ceremony connected food preparation and consumption with obligations to the salmon people.

Salmon was preserved for use beyond the fishing season. In summer, it was wind dried with salt in the Fraser Canyon. In fall, it was smoked, traditionally for a week or two; with modern refrigeration technology, smoking was done for only a few days. Dried salmon was later boiled or steamed before eating. The sources also mention hunting deer, elk, and seals; fishing for stickleback, eulachon, and sturgeon; and gathering shellfish.

Salmon was also important in trade. After the Hudson’s Bay Company established trading posts in Stó꞉lō territory, the company shifted from seeking beaver to requesting salmon. In August 1829, the Stó꞉lō traded Fort Langley 7000 salmon. Between 1830 and 1849, Fort Langley’s purchases of salmon increased from 200 barrels to 2610 barrels.

## Oral tradition & literature

Stó꞉lō culture is based on an oral tradition. The sources describe a continuing connection to the land through accounts of arrival in *S'ólh Téméxw*, ancestral transformations, and the work of *Xexá:ls*, who fixed the world and made it right. The beaver, mountain goat, and sturgeon appear among the ancestral animals and fish associated with these transformations.

The sources also describe the Stó꞉lō as walking simultaneously through the spiritual and physical realms of the landscape, connected to the Creator through the land as transformed by *Xexá:ls*. No named epic, folktale cycle, proverb, riddle, written literary tradition, or contemporary literary revival is identified. The sources state that the smallpox epidemic caused the loss of large amounts of important cultural information through the decimation of the community.

## Language & religion

The traditional language of the Stó꞉lō is Halq'eméylem, the “Upriver dialect” of Halkomelem. It is primarily spoken in Harrison Lake, the lower Fraser Canyon, and the upper and central Fraser Valley, and belongs to the Coast Salish language family. The sources state that there are fewer than five fluent speakers of Halq'eméylem, while there are 278 fluent speakers of the dialects of Halkomelem. The language faces the threat of extinction.

Residential-school students were prohibited from speaking their language and could be punished physically or mentally for using it instead of English. The Stó꞉lō Shxweli Halqʼeméylem Language Program began in 1994 under the education department of the Stó꞉lō Nation's Community Economic Development division. It worked to teach community members, develop curriculum, offer courses through post-secondary institutions, and preserve language through the First Voices mobile and website application. The archive contains 1745 singular words and 667 phrases in Halq'eméylem.

The sources describe a Creator, spiritual and physical realms, *Xexá:ls*, and ancestral transformations.

commons_photos.description: On Wednesday, June 17, Aboriginal Access Services hosted a celebration for UFV students, faculty, and staff, to mark National Aboriginal Day 2015. The event featured dancing, drumming, and singing performances, as well as demos, exhibits, and games organized by members of local Stó:lō and Métis communities.
